  and raw materials far more cheaply than wagons on rutted roads. The United States followed with
  the Erie Canal, completed in 1825. It linked the Hudson River to the Great Lakes, opened the
  Midwest to settlement, and made New York City the country's leading port.

  The nineteenth and early twentieth centuries brought the giant ship canals. The Suez Canal opened
  in 1869 after a decade of work led by Ferdinand de Lesseps. It cut thousands of miles off the
  voyage between Europe and Asia and quickly became a strategic prize. De Lesseps then failed in
  Panama, where disease and difficult terrain defeated the French effort. The United States finished
  the Panama Canal in 1914, using a lock system to lift ships over the isthmus. It changed global
  shipping and cost many lives to build.

  Railways, and later highways, took most freight off the smaller inland canals, and many fell into
  disrepair. In recent decades, restoration groups have brought a lot of them back to life for
  leisure boating, walking, and wildlife. The great ship canals are still vital arteries of world
  trade. From Sumerian ditches to Panama's locks, canals show a steady human ambition to reshape the
  land for the sake of connection.
